paragraph.text_eng: Hello. My name is Strong Thunderbird. I am from the White Earth Reservation. That’s what we’re doing here—I’m making a representation—in what we’re doing. And in regard to that wolf there—he has been admired in what we do. And you should also leave all of the wolves alone. And for us here, in the Indian way, this wolf is admired. And I always tell the children, “Leave that wolf alone. That’s your clan. Leave him alone. Let him roam freely here.” This is also what I am asking of you here. Leave the wolf alone, the wolves here. Thank you.

paragraph.text_eng: I will also try to tell something of what my late father related to me when he raised me. His name was Stands in the South. Well, I was naughty when I was a boy. I was stubborn. And I didn’t always listen well to him when he preached to me.

sentence.sent_text: Gaye niin sa gonaa bangii inga-dibaajim owe minik gekendamaan omaa gaa-nakadamawid aya'aa gaa-niiged nibabaayiban.
Aanish naa gaye niin ingii-gagiibaadiz gaye niin gii-gwiiwizensiwiyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: But I will tell about this one thing that he told me here. These Dakotas came and they were looking for blood here, seeking to retaliate aginst the Ojibwe. They ran into one another here at the river, Battle River [The Place of Slaughter] as it’s called.

sentence.sent_text: Miish o'ow bezhig aya'aa gaa-wiindamawid o'ow ge-wiindamageyaan omaa.

paragraph.text_eng: They must have had a terrible fight, a retributional fight, one where they spilled one another’s blood. They fought to such an extent that their blood just ran together in the river there.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iidog gaa-izhi-miigaadiwaagwen gii-mawine'idiwaad gii-mamiskwiiwanaakanadiwaagwen iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: Then their blood flowed forth to the lake, and out into the lake. Now the Ojibwe live here where the [Dakota] must have camped. And this is where their blood flowed out. That’s why the lake turned this color, from the red plume of blood. And that is how Red Lake received its name. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog omaa gaa-zaagijiwaninig imaa omiskwiimiwaan imaa zaaga'igan o'ow zaaga'iganiing.

paragraph.text_eng: I will try my best to tell what I know of my own roots. For a long time there must have have been Indians here in the village of Ponemah as it’s called.

sentence.sent_text: Aah sa gonaa ingagwe-gashkitoon ayi'ii da-wiindamaageyaan minik gaye niin ezhi-gikendamaan wendakaaneziyaan iidog.
Mii dash iidog mewinzha omaa gii-ayaawag anishinaabeg omaa Obaashiing omaa ezhinikaademagak.

paragraph.text_eng: They arrived at the time of the so called Frenchman. It was to these people that the Indians traded the animals they trapped. So a certain so called French trapper must have also written down what I already know.

sentence.sent_text: Aanish naa omaa gii-dagoshinowag iidog aya'aa wemitigoozhi gaa-izhinikaanind.

paragraph.text_eng: One time the Ojibwe and Dakota must have been starting a war. I’m not sure exactly where they battled one another.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding iidog imaa gii-miigaadiwag omaa anishinaabe miinawaa bwaanan.
Amanj igo dibi go omaa baakaj gaa-tazhiikodaadiwaagwen.

paragraph.text_eng: But there was a certain boy who must have been with the Dakota. So the Ojibwe and Dakota started to go at it when they were here. And it took place here, according to the writings of that one Frenchman.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog a'aa owe bezhig omaa gwiiwizens iidog omaa ogii-wiijiwaan iniw bwaanan iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: It is told in this writing what must have already known. That one boy wasn’t able to run away. That’s this little Dakota, this boy. And so the little Dakota was discovered by the Ojibwe wherever he had been hiding.

sentence.sent_text: Awi'ii wiindamaaged owe ozhibii'igewin gaye wiin aya'aa o'ow sa minik iidog gikendamaan.

Mii dash omaa zhigwa anishinaaben iidog omaa gii-mikaagod iidog omaa dibi go gii-kaazogwen aya'aa bwaanens.

paragraph.text_eng: And he was captured. So from then on that little Dakota started to live in the company of the Ojibwe. He was given a name, and his Indian name was White Thunderbird.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog omaa azhigwa iwe sa gonaa gii-ayaad gii-maaji-wiiji-ayaawaad iniwen anishinaaben a'aw bwaanens.
Aanish naa iidog gii-izhinikaazoban iidog aya'aa Waabi-bines gii-anishinaabewinikaazo.

paragraph.text_eng: He must have eventually married an Ojibwe girl here. And so this little Dakota who was raised here was my great grandfather, and his name was White Thunderbird.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog imaa gaa-izhi-wiidigegwen omaa anishinaabekwen iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s probably why I smell like a Sioux today. That’s it.

paragraph.text_eng: Once, as the story goes, was a martin running along the shore. Then, all of a sudden, he saw a fish. Although he feared it, he fought it. He really wanted that fish. “I wish I could eat it,” he thought. “What am I going to do to kill it?” he thought. Then he ran across the point of land.

paragraph.text_eng: Then next he saw a huge pike, he said to it: “I saw a big pickeral on the other side of this portage. He’s saying all kinds of things about you, he’s sure talking bad about you.”

paragraph.text_eng: Then eventually he said: “I’m going to go fight him.” So then pike swam around to the place. And also that mink ran across the portage again. Then the pike and pickeral fought. Mink watched them fight. And after he saw that they were killing each other, he sang:

paragraph.text_eng: “Leave each other alone, you’ll draw one another’s blood!”
After they had killed one another, he dragged them out of the water. He put them in a hold. And there he lived for a long time.

sentence.sent_text: Apii dash gaa-nisidinid, mii iw gii-ayaagwaadaabaanaad, wiimbakamigaang ogii-paabiindiganaan.

paragraph.text_eng: And when winter came on, he once met a marten, they said they would live together during the winter. Then sure enough, they built a place; and it was from there that they left to go hunting. As for the marten, he hunted rabbits, grouse, squirrels, mice. As for the mink, he only hunted fish. Although they fed each other, the marten gave only a little. He never gave mink a rabbit’s head. So mink was unsatisfied. And as for mink, he didn’t feed marten a fish tail. And so marten was also unsatisfied.

sentence.sent_text: Anii dash eni-biboonining, ningoding ogii-nagishkawaan waabizheshiwan, mii dash ekidowaad maamawi ji-daawaad bibooninig.

paragraph.text_eng: And later, while there was a great northern wind, he cooked some heads. But he didn’t feed mink a tail. Then once, during a great northern wind, mink went out. “Oh, a great wind!” he said.

paragraph.text_eng: ““Where’s the wind coming from?” said the marten.

Then that marten went outside too. “Oh, a great wind!”

paragraph.text_eng: “Where’s the wind coming from?”
“From the part of the fish tail that’s usually eaten, is where the wind is coming from,” said the marten.

sentence.sent_text: "Ozhigwanensan sa ko gii-miijing mii iwidi wendaanimak," ikido waabizheshi.

paragraph.text_eng: When summer came on, they went their separate ways.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s as far as it goes.

Once upon a time, two men were paddling north in their canoe on the sea, there was a great wind; so they were blown out to sea; they didn’t see any land. The wind blew very strong, they didn’t capsize; they continued aimlessly on the sea for a long time. Eventually they were blown ashore. When they landed, they saw the tracks of some mighty being. Since they were scared, they carried their canoe inland, and there they hid underneath it.

sentence.sent_text: Ningoding niizh anishinaabeg bimishkaawaad jiimaaning gichigamiing iwidi giiwedinong inakake, mii iw gaa-izhi-gichi-noodininig; mii dash gaa-izhi-webaashiwaad mizhawagaam gichigamiing; gaawiin ogii-waabandanziinaawaa aki.

paragraph.text_eng: By and by they heard something fall; and when they looked they saw a huge arrow there. So of course they were scared. Soon after they were approached by a great being. They were spoken to by him: “My little brothers, don’t be afraid. I’m called giant. I don’t destroy people,” they were told by him. They saw a caribou hanging from his belt. And that was what the giant was shooting, to eat it.

sentence.sent_text: Ningoding onoondaanaawaa gegoo madwesininig; mii dash inaabiwaad owaabandaanaawaa gichi-bikwak atenig.
Wiiba go ogii-pi-odisigoowaan gichi-anishinaaben, oganoonigoowaan: "Nishiime, gego zegizikegon.
Owaabamaawaan adikwan zhegwazonid, mii wiin iniw bebaapim'waad, wii-amwaad aw misaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: Then they were picked up by him, as the giant was very large. The giant carried the people under his garment. Then they were carried by him back to his place. Then they went in. After a while the wiindigoo went in. Then the wiindigoo said to the giant: “You have people,” he said to him.

paragraph.text_eng: They were hidden by the giant in his house before the wiindigoo came in. “I have no people,” said the giant. “Sure,” said the wiindigoo. Then he could be heard breathing. “Up!” the wiindigoo was sucking in his breath, so eager was he to eat the people. Eventually he became angry, for they were talking for a long time. Eventually the giant became angry too. There was a wooden bowl there inside his house. Then he pried it up with a stick. Then there, there was a puppy under the bowl, the giant’s pet. “Up, Hairless go fight the bad guy.”

sentence.sent_text: Ogii-kaanigowaan biindig endaanid iniw misaaben jibwaa-biindigenid iniw wiindigoon.
ikwanaamod aw wiindigoo, epiichi-misawenimaad anishinaaben wii-amwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Sure enough, the dog got up; shook himself, and then began to get bigger. The more the dog shook, the more he grew.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw geget bazigwiid aw animoons; gii-papawi, mii dash gii-ani-mindidod.

paragraph.text_eng: When he saw that the dog got big, the wiindigoo headed outside. He urged his dog to kill the wiindigoo. So the dog fought the wiindigoo until he killed him. After he had killed him, again he went inside there under the bowl.

paragraph.text_eng: Then they were told by the giant: “My little brothers, I had a purpose for you all to come here. I wanted to see you. Therefore now you may go back home. I’m giving you this little pet of mine. He won’t come back. There are no dogs over there in your country. Maybe you can put him to use. And he acts very much like a human. So then the giant says to his pet: “Come, take home these little brothers of mine!” He carried his little pet to the water. ‘Hairless’ started to grow more. He stood up his pet, and there on his back he placed the people. “There, now take them there, take them straight to where they live!”

sentence.sent_text: Mii idash egoowaad iniw misaaben: "Nishiimeyidog, onjida ingii-inendam ji-bi-izhaayeg omaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Then Hairless took off running. He started getting bigger. He ran through the water, crossing to the other side of the sea. The water was only half way up his leg. Then they were left by the dog, but they were back home.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash gii maajiibatood aw Bashkwadaash, eshkam gii-ani mindido; ogii-aazhawagaamebatoon iw gichi gichigaming; ayaabitawagaad eta gii-akoobii, biinish gii-tagoshing omaa akiing.

paragraph.text_eng: Not until later were they approached by the dog, then they were made up to by him. That’s what happened every where on earth, when the people are approached by a dog. That was the first time dogs were here on earth; they are Hairless’s children.

sentence.sent_text: Baanimaa dash ningoding ogii-odisigowaan animoon, mii go iw gii-pi-inawemigowaad.
Mii go iw miziwe gaa izhiwebak akiing gii-odisigowaad animoshan igiw anishinaabeg.
Mii iw bijiinag apii gii-ayaawaad animoog omaa akiing; mii aw Bashkwadaash oniijaanisan.

paragraph.text_eng: There were many litters of dogs, dogs of various appearances; there are many kinds of the one called dog. All of the dogs come from Hairless, where ever there are dogs today. That’s as far as it goes.

sentence.sent_text: Niibowa daswewaan animoog gii-ayaawag, anooj ezhinaagoziwaad animoshag; niibowa daswewaanagizi aw animosh ezhinikaazod.

paragraph.text_eng: Then another canoe of people went out, and again they saw him. Then, taking his spear, the man speared the sturgeon.

paragraph.text_eng: After he brought it up from the water, he saw a bald eagle clinging to the sturgeon’s head. Then all the people had a big laugh.

paragraph.text_eng: I'll talk about a few more things that happened to us long ago. We never saw white people food; we just ate game meat, ducks and various plants, blueberries and fish. There weren’t any white people yet. There was only the company man, that’s where we got a good deal of what we wore.

paragraph.text_eng: Everything was scarce. sentence.sent_text: Niswi waabizheshiwag, mii iw bezhigwaabik gii-inaginzowaad; zhaangweshiwag niiwin, mii iw bezhigwaabik; waagosh, aapiji wenizhishid, makade-waagosh, niiwaabik eta gii-inaginzo; zhooniyaa-waagosh niizhwaabik eta gii-inaginzo; ojiig bezhigwaabik; bizhiw gaye bezhigwaabik; makwa aapiji wenizhishid niiwaabik; nawaj egaashiinyid niizhwaabik; amik gaye niizhwaabik, egaashiinyid bezhigwaabik; wazhashkwag niishtana, mii iw bezhigwaabik.

paragraph.text_eng: Life was sure hard. Not that it was any easier, the small game was abundant. We never got any money, we only traded for supplies; and they were hard to get.

chapter.eng_title: RESPECT THE INDIAN WAY OF LIFE

paragraph.text_eng: If you live right, you will live a long life. You should remember the great spirit, the one who has given us this life looking after us in a good way. You should give him thanks too. Remember your dreams, sometime you will known the purpose of your dreams. Think things over before you speak. Be patient. Don’t be stingy. Don’t be lazy. Try hard. Don’t be foolish. Don’t fight. Don’t steal. Don’t bother anything. If you fall down, get up again. Know yourself. Take good care of the things you’ve been given. You should laugh at yourself if you make a mistake. Learn something every day. Listen to what you are told, you should remember it too. Live well. Tell the truth. Don’t lie. You are appreciated for who you are. You will be rewarded if you do things right.

sentence.sent_text: Gidaa-mikwenimaa wa'aw gizhe-manidoo, wa'aw miininang o'ow bimaadiziwin weweni ganaweniminang.

paragraph.text_eng: There is strength in the Indian way of life. Carry the Indian way of life, the Indian religion in a proper way. Don’t waste anything. Use everything properly. Everything was made for a reason. Respect the earth. Do not waste anything that has been put on the earth. Respect your body.

sentence.sent_text: Gego gegoo nishibabaamendangen omaa gaa-pagidinigaadeg akiing gaa-ozhitamaagooyang.

paragraph.text_eng: Love one another. Respect each other. Go with each other respectfully. There are people you can go to for help, assistance. Be kind to your fellow people, treat them well. Help and love your fellow Indians. Don’t trouble anyone. Don’t make fun of anyone who is suffering. Don’t talk about anyone. Listen carefully to the elders. You should remember your grandchildren. Respect your fellows in their beliefs. When someone comes to visit you, feed him whatever you have.

sentence.sent_text: Gego awiiya baapinenimaaken gegwaadagitood enigaazid gaye.

paragraph.text_eng: You should be grateful you were born an Indian. You should be thankful for whatever you have.

chapter.eng_title: WHEN THE INDIAN FIRST MET THE WHITE MAN

paragraph.text_eng: This is a story that was told to me by my late grandmother, who went by the name Fanny Johns. My name is Ogimaa-giizhig. I’m from the Caribou Clan. My late grandmother Fanny Johns taught me a little Ojibwe language. This is what she said.

sentence.sent_text: Dibaajimowin o'ow gaa-pi-wiindamawishid nookomisiban, Fanny Johns gaa-izhinikaazod.
Ningii-gikinoo'amaag igo bangii ojibwemowin nookomisiban Fanny Johns.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago, the people lived in the east. They ran away to the deep woods when they saw white men. They were never seen. The whites kept coming back.
Whenever the whites approached, the Indians ran away. The Indians were always very cautious.

sentence.sent_text: Wiikaa gii-naazikaagewaad ingiw chimookomaanag, gii-ginjiba'iwewan anishinaaben.

paragraph.text_eng: One time when the whites came, they poured liquor into wooden bowls at the Indian village. The Indians were still absent from fleeing.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash gii-pi-izhaawaad chimookomaanag, ogii-ziiginaanaawaa ishkodewaaboo imaa mitigo-onaagaansan anishinaabe-oodenaang.

paragraph.text_eng: When the Indians came back, they found the liquor in the bowls. The old time Indians said that it would be bring misfortune and that they should leave it alone. It stunk. Anyways, after they waited for a while one Indian man tried to drink it. He must have become intoxicated. That’s what happened until more Indians took some and became drunk themselves.

sentence.sent_text: Gete-anishnaabeg gii-wiindamaagewag maazhisemagak iw miinawaa daa-boonitoowaad.
Aanawi go ayaapii baabii'owaad, anishinaabewinini bezhig ogii-koji-minikwen.
Mii iw gaa-izhiwebak biinish igo nawaj niibowa anishinaabeg gii-odaapinamowaad, ani-giiwashkwebiiwaad gaye wiinawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Then the white approached again, and made contact with the Indians. They were too drunk to run away. That’s how the whites were able to meet the Indians for the first time. That’s what Fanny Johns said.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-pi-naazikaagewag miinawaa ingiw chimookomaanag, nagishkawaawaad iniw anishinaaben.
Mii keyaa gaa-izhi-gashkitoowaad chimookomaanag ji-nagishkawaawaad iniw anishinaaben nitamising.

paragraph.text_eng: This story was told to me by my friend, Joe B. This is what happened one time when he went hunting long ago. This is what he told me.

sentence.sent_text: Mii o'ow gaa-izhichiged aabiding gii-kiiyosed mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: We were shining one time on the west end of Red Lake. They call it Buck Grove. We used a tractor. On the other side of a field we saw a mooz.

We pointed him out with the light, looking at his large eyes. We used a high-caliber rifle. We saw him moving after we shot. His eyes dropped. It must have been 400 yards away where that moose was seen. We argued about where exactly the moose was over there. Then that moose stood up over there. He was walking dizzily.

sentence.sent_text: Ingii-izhinoo'aanaanig waaswaayaang, mii imaa waabamangwaa omangishkiinzhigweg.
Mii iw niiwaak diba'igaansan gii-waabamind awedi mooz.
Ingii-miigaadimin ganoodamang gwayak eyaad awedi mooz.

paragraph.text_eng: He didn’t die right away. It was a big cow moose. When we shot, the bullet dropped. There deep in her chest beside thr rib cage, the bullet penetrated. I offered tobacco. I put that moose beard out there too. We packed that moose meat out for about two miles. We gave away a lot of meat. We had three deer and one moose.

paragraph.text_eng: Tobacco was put here on earth for the Indian to use. Tobacco was used when an Indian person gave thanks. In the morning too, they used tobacco. Also, tobacco was offered to the one asked to tell legends, only done in the winter. An Indian always offered tobacco to the thunderbirds when they came around. That is why it was known that an Indian was present.

sentence.sent_text: Asemaan gii-pagidinaawan omaa akiing anishinaabe ji-ni-aabaji'aad.
Mii go gaye ezhi-asemaa-zaka'wind a'aw gegwejimind ji-aadizooked, bibooninig eta go.

paragraph.text_eng: In everything an Indian did, he offered tobacco. If he went far, if he was by the water, and if animals were killed, they made an offering. When they saw something unusual, they made a tobacco offering—at waterfalls, huge rocks, mountains—they considered them sacred.

sentence.sent_text: Gakina go gegoo wiin gii-izhichiged aw anishinaabe gii-piindaakoojiged asemaan.
Ingoji waasa gii-izhaad, nibiikaang baa-ayaad gaye, miinawaa awesiinyan gii-nisaawaad, gii-piindaakoonaawaad.
Gegoo mayaginamowaad ogii-piindaakoodoonaawaa—gaakaabikaang, chi-asiniig, wajiwan— ogii-manidoowendaanaawaan.

paragraph.text_eng: When somebody picks his medicine, he certainly makes an offering, putting down his tobacco. And if somebody is picking rice, he certainly makes an offering and puts down tobacco in the water. And if somebody is going to boil sap, he certainly makes an offering. Tobacco is given to somebody who is a gifted speaker when he prays with tobacco. Not everyone knows how. That is why attempts are being made for children to speak Ojibwe to understand the Indian way of life.

sentence.sent_text: Awiiya mamood omashkikiim booch igo biindaakoodood, asemaan odasaan.
Miinawaa manoominiked awiiya, booch igo biindaakoodood asemaan odasaan nibiikaang.
Miinawaa wii-iskigamiziged awiiya, booch igo biindaakojiged.

paragraph.text_eng: The Anishinaabeg of the White Earth Nation are the successors of a great tradition of continental liberty, a native constitution of families, totemic associations. The Anishinaabeg create stories of natural reason, of courage, loyalty, humor, spiritual inspiration, survivance, reciprocal altruism, and native cultural sovereignty.

sentence.sent_text: Gaa-waababiganikaag dazhi-anishinaabeg obimiwiidoonaawaa gaa-izhichigenid ogitiziimiwaan ishkweyaang ji-biitaashkaagoosigwaa bimaadiziwaad, odinawemaaganiwaan, odoodemiwaan.

Geyaabi odibaadodaanaawaa anishinaabeg keyaa enendamowaad, zoongide'ewaad, baapinendamowaad, manidoowendamowaad, zhaabwiiwaad, wiidookawaawaad wiijanishinaabemiwaan, miinawaa go anishinaabe-ogimaawiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: We the Anishinaabeg of the White Earth Nation in order to secure an inherent and essential sovereignty, to promote traditions of liberty, justice, peace, and reserve common resources, and to ensure the inalienable right of native governance for our posterity, do constitute, ordain and establish this Constitution of the White Earth Nation.

sentence.sent_text: Niinawind sa anishinaabewiyaang Gaa-waababiganikaag wii-kanawendamaang keyaa bimiwidooyaang indoogimaawiwininaan, ji-biitaakoshkaagoosiwaang, ji-mino-doodaagooyaang, ji-bizaani-bimaadiziyaang, ji-ganawendamaang indakiiminaan, miinawaa ji-ganawendamaang keyaa ina'oonigooyaang ji-ogimaawiyaang, indinaakonigemin miinawaa indoozitoomin o'ow Ogimaawiwin Enaakonigaadeg Gaa-waababiganikaag.

paragraph.text_eng: There was a beautiful young woman named Waabigwaniins. She was not so much occupied with the same things the other young women her age were interested in. She spent most of her time going on adventures, meeting new people and learning new things. She was very curious about the world around her. And she kept herself very busy most of the time. And this is what made her truly happy.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ojaanimendanzii igiwedi aanind ikwewag ezhi-ojaanimendamowaad.
